body: Sorry, I don't really understand this. Messages aren't queued; they are fired as soon as they are received and the main thread is free.

> If you don't want to stop evaluating what's currently on the stack you can very well make this yourself by wrapping your code in a `setTimeout` and cancel any running timeout in the message handler. This way the next queued message will cancel the previous queued timeout and you'll get only the latest message to be executed. Something like
> 
> ```js
> let timeout = null;
> onmessage = (evt) => {
>   clearTimeout(timeout); // invalidate waiting messages
>   timeout = setTimeout(() => {
>     doSomethingWith(evt.data);
>   }, 1); // 1ms should be enough to deal with a good load of messages
> };
> ```
> 
> ([Live demo](https://worker-pick-last-task.glitch.me))
> 
> Though this exact setup probably means that your Worker would handle a single task, which is not recommended, so you may prefer to handle it from a MessageChannel so that you can handle other tasks "normally" from the same Worker.

Before we have a native active messget getter, this method can work as a hacky workaround. Although 1ms is a reasonably long enough in majority environments nowadays for invalidating a load of queued messages, it's a "hard-code" time based on reality expreience. Also, 1ms is negligible, nevertheless, it would be better to avoid such unnecessary performance lose.

Another hacky workaround that I came up with is using a SharedArrayBuffer object as the latest message ID, which Atomics.add by 1 (as Uint32Array) every time before posting a message (with the current message ID) from the main thread to the worker. Every time the worker thread receives a message, it checks the current message's ID with the latest message ID recorded in the SharedArrayBuffer object, if the two IDs don't equal, then just ignore the current message. But this workaround requires cross-origin isolation set for the site.
